description: Be good at data analysis and visualization.
summary:
Our project is a website that pulls image data from the IRSA and compiles them into organized wavelengths for viewing. The wavelengths are further categorized into human visible light and the remaining infrared spectrum is left to be selected for more advanced/realistic viewing of the raw data. 

Once the data is converted, it is displayed as an interactive map on the left side of the screen with other controls found on the right side. You can search by a "spot in the sky" or "comet or asteroid", as well as view the discovery log to see others' findings. Both view settings have an accompanied infrared band selection, field of view, and image count (frames). There are also recommended objects/locations in case the user just wants to explore for fun. Once an image is selected, you can play them frame by frame, as well as see and quick "before vs. after" jump between frames to help spot a difference. Another function of this website is that if people have new findings they can send it to the website where it can be processed and published once fact checked.  

This addresses the problem by showing the difference between objects location in space over time. This also allows for people to find and interact with the community about what new findings they may have had.
details:
SPHEREx Star Gazing is a free website for flipping through NASA SPHEREx images of the same patch of sky to see what changed, the same method Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto. Visitors search for a star, type coordinates or click the sky map, or follow a comet or asteroid such as 3I/ATLAS, and the site plays every SPHEREx image of it in time order. They can blink between two dates, swipe between them, or use “What changed”, which subtracts the usual sky so only differences remain. Known asteroids are labelled and tracked automatically, and visitors can measure brightness over time and a 102-channel spectrum. Anyone who spots something moving can flag it for a public Discovery log, which the team reviews. Behind the scenes, the server searches NASA/IPAC’s IRSA archive and downloads small cutouts. It removes the dust glow, rotates each cutout north up, lines it up on the stars and shows it on one shared brightness scale. Meanwhile the browser preloads the sequence, so playing and zooming are instant.

Benefits

The site needs no account, installation or astronomy background, and works on phones in English and Spanish. It is honest about raw data: it shows which wavelength each image saw, marks overexposed images and explains cosmic rays. Because known movers are found automatically, first-time visitors see motion right away. Its 3I/ATLAS spectrum shows carbon dioxide gas that matches a published result, and any view can be shared as a link, GIF or video.

Intended impact

SPHEREx collects far more images than scientists can inspect by eye. We want students and hobbyists to watch an interstellar comet cross the stars or a brown dwarf glow in infrared, understand what they see, and learn how astronomers find moving objects. The Discovery log gives them a real, moderated way to contribute.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The server uses Python with FastAPI, astropy and NumPy; the website uses JavaScript with React, Vite, Aladin Lite for the sky map and the HTML canvas. Data comes from NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3), IMCCE’s SkyBoT and CDS Strasbourg, with links to NASA JPL’s Small-Body Database. It runs in Docker on Render’s free plan with a Neon Postgres database, and was tested with pytest, Node’s test runner, headless Chrome and the axe-core accessibility checker. We used Anthropic’s Claude to help write code and translate our site into Spanish; no AI creates or interprets any image or measurement, and the site discloses this.

How it’s creative

It turns Tombaugh’s blink comparator, which found the original “Planet X”, into a one-click tool for modern infrared data. Visitors can view the sky in any of SPHEREx’s 102 wavelength channels, with a legend explaining what each reveals. Difference imaging, star alignment and spectra are calculated live, and the telescope’s colour-changing filters, usually a quirk, become the way spectra are built.

Factors we considered

We prioritised scientific honesty, ease of use for beginners, and accessibility: keyboard control, screen-reader descriptions of motion, blinking under three flashes a second and reduced motion when requested. To stay fast on free hosting we fetch only small cutouts, share downloads between visitors and cache images in the browser, while limiting requests to NASA’s archive. Flagging needs no account, IP addresses are stored only as salted hashes, and names appear only after review.
